structure.title: Table of Contents
structure.summary: This partial document outlines the structure and key components of an SDK, detailing its architecture, security model, and plugin system. It covers the execution model and plugin gateway pipeline, describes five layers of isolation for security, and specifies the agent interface contract including manifest specifications and feedback handling. The document also addresses platform access APIs for state management, knowledge base, history, and LLM connectors, as well as UI rendering contracts for various component types. It explains the plugin output bus for inter-plugin communication, the layout for plugin rendering within the interface, and built-in quick actions across multiple plugins. Additional sections discuss agent manifest control, feedback and analytics mechanisms, the plugin lifecycle from development to monitoring, an alternative open plugin framework, and a summary of key technical decisions.

structure.title: Module 12: Quick Action Agent SDK — Plugin Framework
structure.prefix_summary: This partial document describes Module 12: Quick Action Agent SDK — Plugin Framework. It outlines the purpose of the module, which is to define the SDK and interface contract for building quick action plugins, both built-in and custom. The SDK provides the Agent Interface Contract (including manifest, execute, and feedback), Platform Access APIs for scoped state and knowledge base access, a UI Rendering Contract with Card, Table, and Form templates, eight built-in plugins, inter-plugin communication via a Plugin Output Bus, and a full plugin lifecycle from development to monitoring. The document distinguishes between the MVP (Minimum Viable Product) and full product: the MVP includes only built-in plugins with limited UI and read-only state, while the full product allows tenant developers to create custom plugins, supports state writing, custom UI components, plugin review workflows, a plugin marketplace, and external LLM connectors. The SDK is used by both the internal engineering team and tenant developers, with the only difference being that custom plugins require a review process before activation.

nodes.title: 12.1 SDK Architecture Overview
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.1 SDK Architecture Overview

The Plugin Agent SDK is NOT a standalone library that runs anywhere. It is an interface contract plus a runtime sandbox that lives inside the platform. Think of it like a Shopify App SDK or Slack Bolt framework — you build to a defined interface, and the platform executes your code within its controlled environment. The plugin never runs independently; the Orchestrator (Module 2) invokes it through the Plugin Gateway.

nodes.title: 12.1.1 Execution Model
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes the execution model for plugins within a system managed by an Orchestrator. It outlines the step-by-step process followed when a plugin is triggered, either automatically based on session state or manually by a user. The main points covered include:

1. **Trigger Evaluation:** The Orchestrator checks which plugins should run based on their trigger conditions or manual activation.
2. **Context Assembly:** The Plugin Gateway gathers all necessary context for execution, including required state fields, knowledge base queries, conversation history, previous plugin outputs, and LLM provisioning if needed.
3. **Sandboxed Execution:** Plugins are executed in an isolated environment with strict access controls and time limits.
4. **Output Validation:** The system checks plugin outputs against a declared schema, rejecting invalid outputs and displaying error messages if necessary.
5. **Output Sanitization:** All plugin outputs are sanitized to remove unsafe content before being stored and rendered in the UI.
6. **Analytics Logging:** Execution metrics are logged for monitoring and feedback purposes.

Additionally, the document notes that at session start, all enabled plugins are loaded, and those with auto-surface triggers are evaluated immediately. The plugin load order is independent and does not affect their functionality. The document also includes a code snippet illustrating the execution pipeline within the Plugin Gateway.

nodes.title: 12.2 Security Model — Five Layers of Isolation
nodes.summary: This partial document describes a comprehensive security model for plugin execution, structured around five layers of isolation to prevent plugins from accessing or corrupting data, injecting malicious content, making unauthorized network calls, or escalating permissions. The five layers are: (1) Sandboxed Execution, isolating plugin runtime environments; (2) Scoped API Access, restricting plugins to a controlled API with enforced permissions and rate limits; (3) State Write Sandboxing, limiting plugins to write only within their own namespace; (4) Output Sanitization, ensuring plugin outputs are safe for UI rendering and free from XSS or injection risks; and (5) Review Gate, requiring custom plugins to pass security reviews before activation. The document also details rate limiting per plugin execution and clarifies that the Plugin Gateway, responsible for enforcing these controls, is integrated within the Orchestrator module rather than as a separate service, leveraging existing infrastructure for efficiency and scalability.

nodes.title: 12.3.1 The Manifest
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the structure and purpose of a plugin manifest within a platform. It details that every plugin, whether built-in or custom, is defined by a manifest—a JSON document specifying key attributes. The manifest includes the plugin’s identity, version, and description, as well as its trigger conditions (when and how it activates), manual and automatic surfacing options, and priority in the user interface. It outlines required state and knowledge base data, conversation history depth, and LLM (large language model) configuration. The manifest also defines the expected output schema, permissions for reading and writing state and knowledge base data, resource limits (such as execution time and API call quotas), and the types of user feedback collected. An example manifest for an email generation plugin is provided, illustrating these fields in practice.

nodes.title: 12.3.2 Manifest Field Reference
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the "Manifest Field Reference" for plugins, detailing the required and optional fields that define a plugin's behavior, permissions, and integration within a platform. It outlines each manifest field, specifying its type, purpose, and who is responsible for setting or overriding it (developer, tenant admin, or platform). Key points include unique plugin identification, trigger conditions (automatic and manual), display priority, state and knowledge base requirements, conversation history access, LLM (large language model) usage, output schema, explicit permissions, resource limits, and feedback collection. The document emphasizes security, customization, and governance, noting which fields are immutable, which can be overridden, and how enforcement and review processes work.

nodes.title: 12.3.3 The execute() Function
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the execute() function within a plugin system. The function serves as the main logic handler for the plugin, receiving a PluginContext object that provides access to provisioned state fields, knowledge base (KB) search capabilities, conversation history, LLM (large language model) client, and outputs from other plugins. The function demonstrates how to:

- Access customer profile and agent recommendation data from the plugin state.
- Retrieve competitor comparison data from another plugin’s output.
- Query a knowledge base for relevant case studies based on customer industry and recommended products.
- Generate an email draft using a built-in LLM connector, leveraging the gathered data.
- Return a structured form output containing fields for recipient email, subject, tone selection, and email body, along with actions such as copying the draft or regenerating it.

The section provides a code example illustrating these steps, emphasizing integration between state management, inter-plugin communication, knowledge retrieval, and LLM-powered content generation within the plugin framework.

nodes.title: 12.3.4 The onFeedback() Handler
nodes.summary: This partial document explains the purpose and implementation of the onFeedback() handler in a plugin system. It highlights that onFeedback is an optional, session-scoped function designed for real-time adaptation based on user interactions (such as dismiss, edit, or regenerate actions) with the plugin’s output. The handler allows the plugin to adjust its behavior for the next execution within the same session, for example, by tracking regeneration attempts or significant edits. The document contrasts onFeedback with the Module 16 Feedback Engine, clarifying that while onFeedback enables immediate, ephemeral adjustments within a session, Module 16 is responsible for persistent, long-term learning and systemic improvements across all sessions and users. Both mechanisms use the same feedback signals, but onFeedback processes them first for instant adaptation, and Module 16 aggregates them for strategic changes.

nodes.title: 12.4.1 State Read API — What Plugins Can and Cannot Read
nodes.summary:
This partial document outlines the "State Read API" permissions for plugins, specifying which data fields plugins can and cannot access. It presents a table listing various data paths, indicating their readability, and providing rationales for each. Key points include:

- Plugins can read core customer context (profile, products, contacts), computed enrichment metrics, agent recommendations, conversation phase, talking points, discovery progress, intent signals, their own plugin state, and other plugins’ rendered outputs.
- Plugins are explicitly denied access to sensitive fields such as authentication tokens, platform configuration, other plugins’ private state, system prompts, and raw database access.
- The rationale for each permission emphasizes security, data boundaries, and the principle that plugins operate on pre-aggregated, non-sensitive data, with strict separation from platform internals and credentials.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 State Write API
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the "State Write API" for plugins, outlining the rules and restrictions for plugin state modifications. It distinguishes between the MVP phase, where plugins are strictly read-only, and the full product phase, where plugins are allowed to perform sandboxed writes only to their own state namespace (plugin_state.{own_plugin_id}.*). The document provides a table listing various possible write targets, specifying whether writes are allowed and giving example use cases or reasons for prohibition. Only writes to a plugin’s own state are permitted (in the full product), enabling features like saving drafts or audit data. All other targets—including agent state, discovery progress, customer data, workflow control, recommendations, and intent signals—are strictly disallowed to prevent corruption, confusion, or security issues, with explanations for each restriction.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 KB Query API and History Read API
nodes.summary:
### 12.4.3 KB Query API and History Read API

KB Query API: The plugin provides a search query string and optional filters (source type, max results). The Plugin Gateway routes the query to the tenant’s Foundry IQ Knowledge Base (Module 3) with the tenant’s retrieval effort setting. Results come back as title + content snippet + relevance score. The plugin CANNOT modify, add, or delete KB entries. Read-only.

History Read API: The plugin receives the last N messages of the current conversation (N = conversationHistoryDepth from manifest, max 50). Messages include role (user/assistant), content, and timestamp. System prompts are stripped. The plugin CANNOT read conversations from other sessions, other reps, or other tenants.

nodes.title: 12.4.4 LLM Connector
nodes.summary:
This partial document section describes the "LLM Connector" for plugins requiring natural language generation. It outlines how plugins declare their need for LLM access and how the SDK facilitates this via a context.llm.call() function. The document compares the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) and Full Product versions across several aspects:

- LLM Source: MVP uses only a built-in connector with the tenant’s configured model, while the Full Product allows plugins to specify external LLM providers via manifest, subject to gateway whitelisting.
- Token Tracking: Both versions track tokens per plugin execution for analytics and billing, but the Full Product adds per-plugin token budgets and tenant-configurable monthly limits.
- Prompt Injection Protection: Both versions wrap plugin prompts to prevent overriding platform instructions; the Full Product adds automated prompt scanning during review.
- Streaming: MVP does not support streaming (plugins receive complete responses), while the Full Product allows plugins to opt into streaming for progressive UI rendering.

A decision summary explains that MVP restricts LLM access to the built-in connector for cost, consistency, and security, while the Full Product enables external connectors for specialized use cases, maintaining oversight through manifest declarations and gateway controls.

nodes.title: 12.5 UI Rendering Contract
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.5 UI Rendering Contract

| Design Principle Plugins output STRUCTURED DATA. The platform renders it. This separation ensures consistent UX across all plugins, prevents UI injection attacks, enables the platform to adapt rendering for different devices (desktop sidebar vs. mobile sheet), and allows the platform to evolve its design system without breaking plugins. A plugin never outputs HTML — it outputs JSON that the platform’s rendering engine transforms into UI components. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.5.1 Card Template
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Card Template," which is the main output format for displaying structured information in a panel. The card includes a title, optional subtitle, icon, status indicator, multiple content sections, and action buttons. Sections can be styled as plain text, key-value pairs, bullet lists, or highlighted callout boxes. The example provided shows a competitor comparison between Cisco and Aruba, with sections for key differentiators, price comparison, and recommended positioning. Action buttons such as "Copy to Email" and "Dismiss" are included, and the card can be pinned, dismissed, or expanded in the Side Panel. The document also explains how section styles are rendered and notes that the platform’s design system controls the visual appearance.

nodes.title: 12.5.2 Table Template
nodes.summary: The partial document explains the Table Template, which is used to render structured comparison grids and tabular data for scenarios like product comparisons, tier upsells, feature matrices, and quote generation. It describes how core agents supply comparison data, which the plugin formats into a table for display. An example is provided showing a tier comparison between Standard and Premium, highlighting features, pricing, and actionable options such as copying the table to an email.

nodes.title: 12.5.3 Form Template
nodes.summary: The partial document explains the "Form Template" used in plugins that require user input, not just display output. It describes how plugins can pre-populate form fields (using LLM generation or data assembly), allowing users (reps) to edit before submitting. Upon submission or action, the form data is sent back to the plugin’s execute() function or handled by built-in actions like copy_to_clipboard or re_execute. Example use cases include editing email drafts, generating quotes, and custom data entry forms. The document details the JSON structure for a form, including field types (text, textarea, email, number, dropdown, checkbox, date, hidden), field properties (id, type, label, value, required, options, placeholder, validation), and supported actions.

nodes.title: 12.5.4 File Output
nodes.summary:
### 12.5.4 File Output

Some plugins produce downloadable files rather than (or in addition to) inline UI. Generate Quote produces a formatted quote document. Meeting Prep Brief might produce a printable one-page brief. The file output type returns a file reference that the UI renders as a download button.

| { "type": "file", "filename": "Quote_AcmeManufacturing_2026-03-04.pdf", "mimeType": "application/pdf", "data": "<base64-encoded-content>", "preview": {  // Optional inline preview card "type": "card", "title": "Quote: Acme Manufacturing", "sections": [{ "heading": "Summary", "content": "3 line items, total $24,500", "style": "text" }], "actions": [{ "label": "Download PDF", "action": "download_file" }] } } |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.5.5 Custom Component (Full Product Only)
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the strategy for supporting custom UI components in a plugin platform. It explains that while the MVP (Minimum Viable Product) only allows plugins to use predefined Card, Table, Form, and File templates—ensuring security, consistent user experience, and simplified development—the full product will support custom React components for advanced use cases. These custom components run inside a tightly sandboxed iframe with strict security controls (limited permissions, no external resource loading, and communication only via postMessage). The review process for such plugins is more stringent, including security scanning and size limits. The rationale is to cover most needs with safe, simple templates, reserving custom components for complex, interactive scenarios that require greater flexibility.

nodes.title: 12.6 Plugin Output Bus — Inter-Plugin Communication
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the Plugin Output Bus, a mechanism for inter-plugin communication within a session. It allows plugins to access the rendered output (such as cards, tables, or forms) of other plugins in a read-only manner, without exposing private plugin state or creating dependencies. The Orchestrator maintains a session-wide object where sanitized plugin outputs are stored and accessible. Plugins can reference each other's outputs to enhance their own functionality (e.g., including competitor data in an email), but cannot modify, invoke, or depend on the execution order of other plugins. If a plugin’s output is unavailable, the reading plugin proceeds gracefully without it.

nodes.title: 12.7 Rep Interface Layout — Where Plugins Render
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the interface layout for a representative (rep) workflow, focusing on where plugins render within the UI. It describes the main UI zones: the Customer Context Panel (left, always visible, core customer info, not plugin-enabled), the Accepted Products Tray (bottom left or floating, shows selected products, not plugin-enabled but read by plugins for quoting), the Chat Panel (center, main conversation area, plugins do not render here except when referenced by core agents), the Side Panel (right, collapsible, primary zone for plugin outputs like cards, tables, forms, with controls for managing outputs), and the Quick Action Bar (bottom, plugin trigger buttons, some always visible, others contextual). It also mentions the Product Catalog Browser, which in the full product allows reps to manually browse and add products, supporting workflows beyond AI recommendations. The document clarifies which UI zones are core components versus plugin integration points, and how plugin outputs and triggers are managed within the interface.

nodes.title: 12.8 Built-In Quick Actions — All 8 Plugins
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.8 Built-In Quick Actions — All 8 Plugins

All 8 built-in plugins are built on the same SDK described above. They are NOT special — they use the same manifest, execute function, Plugin Gateway, and rendering templates as any custom plugin. This section specifies each plugin’s trigger, data diet, output, LLM usage, and evolution during a conversation.

nodes.title: 12.8.1 Availability and Trigger Matrix
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the "Availability and Trigger Matrix" for various plugins within a platform. It presents a table detailing when each plugin's button is visible, the conditions under which each plugin auto-triggers, the phases in which they appear, whether they use a large language model (LLM), and their priority order. Plugins covered include KB Search, Account Overview, Meeting Prep Brief, Competitor Comparison, Find Case Study, Generate Email, Generate Quote, and Objection Handler. The document also explains how the system handles simultaneous plugin triggers: all relevant plugins are shown in the side panel, ordered by priority, allowing the user to choose which to engage with, rather than the system making the selection.

nodes.title: 12.8.2 Per-Plugin Specification
nodes.summary:
This partial document section outlines the specifications for several plugins within a sales or customer engagement platform. Each plugin’s purpose, data sources, triggers, and output formats are described in detail:

- **KB Search**: A simple retrieval plugin that routes user queries to a knowledge base, returning relevant results as clickable cards. It uses customer profile and recent conversation context to improve relevance and is always available but never auto-triggered.
- **Account Overview**: Aggregates and formats pre-computed customer and enrichment data (e.g., health score, revenue trends, whitespace, benchmarks) into a card for quick reference. It auto-surfaces at session start for known customers.
- **Meeting Prep Brief**: Uses an LLM to synthesize a narrative briefing for upcoming calls, incorporating customer data, enrichment fields, previous session summaries, and relevant case studies. It auto-surfaces if the customer hasn’t been contacted recently.
- **Competitor Comparison**: Triggered by competitor mentions, this plugin gathers competitor intel and customer product data, then uses an LLM to generate feature comparisons, differentiators, and talk tracks, outputting both tables and highlight cards.
- **Find Case Study**: Retrieves and displays relevant case studies based on customer industry and discovery signals, using semantic search without LLM involvement. It auto-surfaces when a use case or industry need is detected.
- **Generate Email**: The most LLM-intensive plugin, it drafts personalized emails using customer, contact, recommendation, and conversation data, as well as outputs from other plugins. The draft is editable and frequently refined by users.
- **Generate Quote**: Assembles structured quotes from accepted recommendations and pricing data, outputting a card and file preview. It is template-based and does not use LLMs, with PDF generation planned for future versions.
- **Objection Handler**: Triggered by detected objections, it uses LLMs to generate multiple counter-arguments (fact-based, value reframing, social proof) and provides actionable responses for the user.

Overall, the document details how each plugin operates, what data it consumes, how it is triggered, and the structure of its outputs, emphasizing the integration of retrieval, data assembly, and LLM-based synthesis to support sales and customer engagement workflows.

nodes.title: 12.8.3 Data Diet Summary
nodes.summary: This partial document provides a summary table of various plugins used in a system, detailing their data usage and operational parameters. For each plugin, it lists the state fields accessed, the knowledge base (KB) sources referenced, the depth of historical data considered (in terms of message count), and the typical number of LLM (large language model) tokens processed. The plugins covered include KB Search, Account Overview, Meeting Prep Brief, Competitor Comparison, Find Case Study, Generate Email, Generate Quote, and Objection Handler. The table highlights how each plugin interacts with customer data, enrichment sources, and external knowledge bases, as well as their typical data and token requirements.

nodes.title: 12.8.4 Deployment Strategy
nodes.summary:
### 12.8.4 Deployment Strategy

| DECISION: All Built-In Plugins Bundled in Orchestrator Service Decided: All 8 built-in plugins run within the Orchestrator service (Module 2), executed by the Plugin Gateway. They are NOT separate microservices. Each plugin is a function invocation, not a persistent process. Rationale: Plugins are short-lived (< 5 seconds), stateless functions. Deploying 8 separate services for 8 small functions is massive over-engineering — 8 Kubernetes pods, 8 pipelines, 8 health checks for functions that run 2–3 seconds each. The Plugin Gateway handles isolation via sandboxed execution contexts. Built-in code is trusted. Custom plugins in full product MAY run in isolated containers (Lambda/Azure Functions) because we don’t trust external code, but built-in plugins always execute in-process. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.9 Agent Manifest Control — Versioning, Customization, and Deployment
nodes.prefix_summary: ## 12.9 Agent Manifest Control — Versioning, Customization, and Deployment

nodes.title: 12.9.1 Where Manifests Live
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains where plugin manifest files are stored and managed within the system. It distinguishes between built-in plugins, whose manifests are checked into the codebase and registered automatically during deployment, and custom plugins, whose manifests are uploaded via the Admin Portal and associated with specific tenants. Both types of manifests are stored in the plugin_registry database table, with custom plugin code bundles stored in tenant-specific Blob Storage. The section also provides the schema for the plugin_registry table, detailing fields such as plugin_id, tenant_id, version, manifest, status, code_bundle_url, and audit information.

nodes.title: 12.9.2 Are Built-In Plugins Domain-Specific?
nodes.summary: This partial document section addresses whether built-in plugins are domain-specific. It explains that built-in plugins are intentionally domain-agnostic, functioning the same way across various industries such as IT reselling, insurance, and food distribution. The plugins' logic remains universal, while the data they process is specific to each tenant or domain. Domain-specific behavior is achieved through external mechanisms: (1) tenant-specific prompt modifiers that adjust the language model's context, (2) enforcement of tenant business rules by an orchestrator before and after plugin execution, and (3) tenant-specific knowledge base content. Thus, the plugins themselves do not change per domain; only the data and contextual inputs do.

nodes.title: 12.9.3 Tenant Customization — Three Levels
nodes.summary:
This partial document section outlines the three levels of tenant customization available in a multi-tenant plugin system:

1. **Level 1: Prompt Modifiers** — Tenants can adjust the behavior of built-in plugins by modifying prompts (e.g., tone, terminology, domain-specific instructions). These changes are made via configuration, not code, and are stored per tenant. No code deployment or branching is required.

2. **Level 2: Template Overrides** — Tenants can customize the output structure of plugins (e.g., form fields, card sections, table columns) by overriding templates through configuration. This is also stored per tenant and does not require code changes or branching.

3. **Level 3: Custom Plugin Fork** — Tenants can develop and deploy their own custom plugins, replacing built-in ones if needed. These custom plugins are fully tenant-owned and maintained, stored separately, and do not affect the main codebase.

The document emphasizes that all tenant-specific behavior is achieved through configuration or independent custom plugins, eliminating the need for code branches or per-tenant versions. Updates to built-in plugins are applied universally, with tenant configurations automatically integrated, avoiding merge conflicts and versioning complexity.

Additionally, the document explains how tenants can enable or disable specific plugins at both the tenant and user level through configuration settings, allowing for further customization without code changes.

nodes.title: 12.10 Feedback and Analytics — What We Collect and How We Use It
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.10 Feedback and Analytics — What We Collect and How We Use It

| Connection to Module 16 Plugin analytics feed into Module 16 (Feedback Engine), which is the platform’s unified feedback processing system. This section defines WHAT signals plugins generate. Module 16 defines HOW those signals are aggregated, analyzed, and used for system-wide improvement. The signals defined here are the plugin-specific subset of Module 16’s full signal taxonomy. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.10.1 Signal Taxonomy
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines a taxonomy of signals collected from plugin usage within a software platform. It categorizes signals into Execution Metrics, Engagement Signals, Edit Signals, Dismiss Reasons, and Outcome Correlation, detailing the specific data points collected, how they are gathered (e.g., automatically by the system or via UI tracking), and their intended purposes such as system health monitoring, performance optimization, plugin usefulness assessment, output quality evaluation, and measuring the ROI of plugins. Additionally, the document describes mechanisms for tracking LLM (Large Language Model) token usage and associated costs, allowing tenant administrators to monitor and set monthly token budgets for each plugin. If a plugin exceeds its token budget, it automatically switches to a less costly, template-based output mode, notifying the user of the change.

nodes.title: 12.10.2 How Feedback Improves Plugins
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains how user and system feedback mechanisms are used to improve plugin performance and user experience. It outlines several feedback loops at different timeframes: real-time adjustments within a session via automatic handlers, weekly manual reviews of aggregated metrics by engineers, automated proposals for changes based on detected usage patterns, and A/B testing of prompt versions to determine the most effective approach. The table details the actors involved, the mechanisms for collecting and acting on feedback, and provides concrete examples for each scenario.

nodes.title: 12.11.1 Step 1: Develop
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the first step in plugin development, detailing the implementation of three key files: manifest.json (which defines the plugin’s contract, including triggers, permissions, resources, output schema, and feedback signals), execute.ts (the main function containing business logic and returning structured output), and an optional onFeedback.ts (for real-time session feedback). It explains the role of the SDK in providing TypeScript types and API clients, and notes that developers use @sip/plugin-sdk for type checking, with the runtime SDK supplied by the Plugin Gateway.

nodes.title: 12.11.2 Step 2: Test
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Plugin Test Harness," a local CLI tool included in the @sip/plugin-sdk for testing plugins before deployment. It outlines the process of loading mock context data, executing the plugin against this data, and validating the output against the declared schema. The harness checks for permission compliance by ensuring plugins only access permitted fields, measures execution time against performance limits, and supports both mock and real LLM calls for testing. It also emphasizes edge case testing by simulating scenarios like missing data or timeouts to ensure robust plugin behavior. The document includes an example CLI test run, showing schema validation, permission checks, performance metrics, and edge case handling, concluding that all tests must pass before plugin registration.

nodes.title: 12.11.3 Step 3: Register
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.3 Step 3: Register

Built-in plugins: Registration is automatic. The CI/CD pipeline reads /plugins/*/manifest.json and upserts into plugin_registry. Status is set to ‘active’ immediately (no review gate for built-in).

Custom plugins (full product): Tenant admin uploads the plugin bundle (manifest + code) via Admin Portal. The bundle is validated (schema compliance, size limits, required fields). The manifest is parsed and inserted into plugin_registry with status: ‘pending_review.’

nodes.title: 12.11.4 Step 4: Review (Full Product Custom Plugins Only)
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.4 Step 4: Review (Full Product Custom Plugins Only)

Built-in plugins skip this step entirely. Custom plugins undergo review before activation:

Manifest audit: Does it declare only the permissions it actually needs? Is externalNetwork: true justified? Are resource limits reasonable?

Code review: Does the code do what the manifest says? Any hidden API calls? Any data exfiltration attempts? Any attempt to access DOM or browser APIs?

Security scan: Automated static analysis for common vulnerabilities: injection patterns, eval() usage, external URL construction, obfuscated code.

Test results: Did it pass the test harness? All edge cases handled? Performance within limits?

Review result: approved (status changes to ‘approved’, can be activated by tenant admin) or rejected with specific feedback for the developer to address.

nodes.title: 12.11.5 Step 5: Deploy / Activate
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.5 Step 5: Deploy / Activate

Built-in plugins: Deployed with every platform release. Available to all tenants. Whether a specific plugin is ENABLED for a tenant depends on tenant_config.agent_config.quick_action_ids.

Custom plugins: After approval, tenant admin activates the plugin in Admin Portal. Status changes from ‘approved’ to ‘active.’ The Orchestrator’s plugin trigger evaluation now includes this plugin for this tenant’s sessions.

Rollback: If a plugin update introduces a regression, the previous version can be re-activated. plugin_registry stores version history. Rollback = deactivate current version, activate previous version. One database update, immediate effect for new sessions.

nodes.title: 12.11.6 Step 6: Monitor
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the monitoring process for plugin execution within a system. It details the metrics tracked for each plugin, including usage frequency, dismissal rate, edit rate for form plugins, error rate, and LLM (Large Language Model) cost. The document explains how these metrics are displayed on an admin dashboard and used to flag issues such as high dismissal or error rates. It also describes an automated circuit breaker mechanism that temporarily disables a plugin after repeated failures within a session, ensuring system stability and alerting administrators to potential problems.

nodes.title: 12.12 Alternative Architecture: Open Plugin Framework
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.12 Alternative Architecture: Open Plugin Framework

| Why This Section Exists The Controlled Framework (Sections 12.1–12.11) prioritizes safety, consistency, and predictability. It is the recommended approach for MVP and early full product. However, as the platform matures and the developer ecosystem grows, a more open framework may be warranted. This section presents an alternative architecture that trades some control for developer freedom. The constraint is: security isolation and analytics collection remain mandatory. Everything else is negotiable. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.12.1 Philosophy Shift
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines a shift in philosophy between a "Controlled Framework" and an "Open Framework" for plugin and platform architecture. It compares key dimensions such as UI output, LLM access, state access, plugin-to-plugin communication, review process, and resource limits. The Controlled Framework restricts plugins to predefined UI templates, mediates all LLM calls, enforces strict state access and manual reviews, and imposes hard resource limits. In contrast, the Open Framework allows plugins to output custom React components, choose their own LLMs, access broader state fields, directly invoke other plugins, undergo automated reviews for low-risk plugins, and operate under more flexible resource limits. Security and orchestration mechanisms are highlighted, with sandboxing and circular dependency detection in place.

nodes.title: 12.12.2 Open Framework Security Model
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the Open Framework Security Model, emphasizing three non-negotiable constraints: (1) Tenant Data Isolation, ensuring plugins cannot access data from other tenants through strict database, API, and execution-level controls; (2) Mandatory Analytics Collection, requiring all plugin executions to generate analytics signals via an enforced instrumentation wrapper, with plugins unable to bypass or tamper with this process; and (3) Output Sanitization, mandating that plugin outputs are rendered in a secure iframe sandbox, preventing access to the parent application's DOM, cookies, localStorage, and external resources, thereby isolating plugin effects.

nodes.title: 12.12.3 Open Framework LLM Access
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes how, within an open framework, plugins can use their own Large Language Models (LLMs) instead of relying solely on the platform’s built-in LLM connector. Plugins can import any LLM SDK (such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cohere) and manage their own encrypted API keys. They can also use fine-tuned or domain-specific models tailored to their needs. All LLM calls—whether to the built-in or external models—are automatically wrapped by the platform’s instrumentation layer, which logs details like model used, token usage, latency, and cost, ensuring transparency and monitoring. For security, any external LLM endpoints must be declared in the plugin manifest and are whitelisted by the Plugin Gateway, with all outbound requests logged. Tenant administrators can monitor which plugins make external LLM calls, and tenants with strict data residency requirements can disable external LLM access entirely.

nodes.title: 12.12.4 Open Framework State Access
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes changes in the open framework regarding plugin state access. It explains that plugins now have broader read permissions, allowing them to access entire namespaces (such as customer.*, enrichment.*, and intent_signals.*) without specifying individual fields, though sensitive fields remain protected. It introduces a shared plugin namespace (plugin_shared.*) for inter-plugin communication, with last-write-wins conflict resolution. The document also clarifies that certain core state namespaces (agent_state.*, discovery.*, active_workflow, recommendations.*) remain strictly protected and are never writable by plugins.

nodes.title: 12.12.5 Migration Path: Controlled to Open
nodes.summary:
This partial document outlines the phased migration strategy for a platform transitioning from a controlled to an open framework. It describes three main phases: 

1. **Phase 1 (MVP):** Launches with a controlled framework, supporting only built-in plugins and templates, with no custom plugins or write access, to validate the SDK and establish a secure baseline.
2. **Phase 2 (Full Product v1):** Introduces custom plugin development by tenant developers using a controlled SDK, with manual review and sandboxed write access, allowing for limited extensibility while maintaining security.
3. **Phase 3 (Full Product v2):** Expands to an open framework with broader state access, external LLM connectors, a plugin message bus, automated security scanning, and a shared plugin namespace, contingent on real-world usage and security benchmarks.

The document emphasizes that the initial controlled framework is chosen for safety and simplicity, with the architecture designed to allow a seamless transition to an open model based on proven demand and security performance.

nodes.title: 12.13 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary:
This partial document summarizes key technical decisions for a plugin SDK and platform architecture. The main points covered include: 

- The SDK is defined as an interface contract (TypeScript types and test harness), not a standalone library or service, ensuring simple deployment and reliable permission enforcement.
- Both built-in and custom plugins use the same SDK interface, with no privileged access or backdoors for built-in plugins, fostering trust and robustness.
- Plugins are designed to be domain-agnostic, with domain-specific behavior injected at runtime via tenant configuration, avoiding the complexity of maintaining multiple plugin versions for different industries.
- The MVP uses template-based UI components (Card, Table, Form, File) for most use cases, with support for custom React components planned for the full product once security infrastructure is mature.
- All plugin feedback is routed to a unified Feedback Engine, enabling cross-component pattern detection and avoiding fragmented feedback processing.
- The framework will start as a controlled SDK for MVP and early releases, with plans to open it up later based on demand and security track record, prioritizing safety and incremental permission expansion.
